narrative:
The model estimated a 59.6% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, it judged failure slightly more likely than passing, and that result led to your law-school application being denied. This is a screening estimate, not a certainty, but it was strong enough to affect the admission decision.

The decision was driven most by your undergraduate GPA, which ranked as the strongest factor and tilted the prediction toward failure. Your 3.30 GPA is slightly above the 3.23 average among accepted students, so this was not a weak academic record in isolation; still, in the model’s overall assessment it was the leading risk signal. The second most influential factor was your third-year class standing: your decile of 9 is much higher than the accepted-student average of 5.79, and this factor pushed toward passing—the main point in your favor. Third was your LSAT score. Your score of 40 is above the accepted-student average of 37.18, but this factor nonetheless leaned toward failure.

Next, ask the admissions office for feedback and whether any review or reconsideration is available. If feasible, retake the LSAT, strengthen your academic record or add relevant legal experience, and apply to programs with strong bar-passage support. If you enroll elsewhere, begin bar preparation early and use academic support services.
